title: Twelve people, twelve prompts
scenario:
You lead a content team of 12 at a marketing agency. Everyone uses an AI assistant daily, but each person writes their own prompts. A key client complained that the tone of their newsletters changes from week to week, depending on who wrote the draft. Your director asks you to set up a team playbook.

The exhibit shows what you found in your first week.
exhibit:
Findings, week 1

- Most common tasks: client newsletters, social posts, meeting summaries.
- 12 different newsletter prompts in personal chat histories.
  2 of them get good results; the rest are one line long.
- Last month someone edited the only shared prompt and deleted its examples.
  Drafts were weak for a week before anyone noticed.
- IT plans to move the team to a newer model next month.
- A teammate found a free "brand voice" Skill on a public forum and wants to install it.

questions.prompt: How should you start the playbook?

options.text: Write one big master prompt that covers newsletters, social posts and summaries together.
options.explanation: One prompt for three different tasks mixes their formats and checks. Each common task needs its own play.

options.text: Turn the 2 good newsletter prompts into one play with a template, examples, a checklist and an owner.
options.explanation: Right. Start with the most common task and the prompts that already work. Then add the other common tasks the same way.

options.text: Let each person keep their own prompt, but ask them all to try harder to match the client's tone of voice.
options.explanation: That keeps twelve different setups, which is the cause of the uneven tone the client noticed.

options.text: Move the whole team to the most capable model first, and only build a playbook if problems remain.
options.explanation: A stronger model still gets twelve different briefs. The tone varies because the briefs vary.

questions.prompt: How do you stop a silent bad edit, like the deleted examples, from happening again?

options.text: Lock the playbook so that nobody, not even the owner, can ever change a play again.
options.explanation: Plays need to improve over time. The aim is careful change, not no change.

options.text: Ask the model to check each new draft and tell you if the prompt behind it has been changed by anyone.
options.explanation: The model only sees the prompt it is given. It can't tell you what an earlier version said.

options.text: Name one owner per play, keep a change log, and run saved test cases before a change goes live.
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI's guide says to treat prompts like code: review changes, keep history, and run tests every time you publish.

options.text: Send a reminder email to the whole team each month asking them to be careful when editing.
options.explanation: A reminder does not catch a bad edit. A test before publishing does.

questions.prompt: IT moves the team to a newer model next month. What should happen to the plays?

options.text: Run each play's saved test cases on the new model and fix any play that fails before switching.
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI's guide says different model versions can give different results. Anthropic's guide says to re-check techniques against your own tests on a new model.

options.text: Nothing. A newer model is better at every task, so every play will work at least as well as before.
options.explanation: Newer does not guarantee the same behavior on your prompts. Test before you switch.

options.text: Delete all the plays and write new ones from scratch, because old prompts never suit new models.
options.explanation: That throws away tested work. Most plays may pass. Test them and fix only what fails.

options.text: Ask IT to cancel the move, so the team stays on the old model and never has to re-test the plays.
options.explanation: Avoiding every upgrade is not a plan. A playbook with saved tests makes an upgrade safe to check, instead of something to fear.

questions.prompt: What do you say about the free "brand voice" Skill from the public forum?

options.text: Install it right away. It is free, and Skills are only text, so they can't cause any harm.
options.explanation: Anthropic's docs say a malicious Skill can direct the model to act in ways that don't match its stated purpose.

options.text: Install it, but only for the teammate who found it, so the risk stays with one person.
options.explanation: One person's account can still have access to client data. The risk is the unknown source, not the number of users.

options.text: Install it if many people on the forum have liked it, since popular Skills are reviewed by others.
options.explanation: Popularity is not a security review. Anthropic's docs say to use Skills only from trusted sources.

options.text: Don't install it as is. Use trusted sources only, and review any Skill like software first.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic's docs say to use Skills from trusted sources and to audit any other Skill thoroughly before use.
